description: Width tiers for Design and Technologies Years 3-4 (ACARA v9). Covers all 9 descriptors in the Y3-4 band.
subject: Design and Technologies

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest engagement that satisfies the descriptor's command term. For K-strand standards (describe, examine): minimum engages with at least one concrete example that genuinely meets the command term. For P-strand standards (explore, generate, select, use, evaluate, sequence): minimum completes the capability in at least one context. Minimum is not what's easy — it is what's sufficient.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope grounded in the most common elaboration cases. What a class that has engaged with the descriptor well would have done. Covers the range of contexts and examples ACARA intended without requiring every elaboration.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, contexts or task variants — not harder versions of the same context. For K-strand: more phenomena, production contexts and cultural perspectives. For P-strand: more task types, materials, design contexts and scales of production. First Nations directions from elaborations always included.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are used as the primary source for typical_width and to identify First Nations wider directions. Minimum is set by the descriptor's command term, not by elaboration examples. Wider may infer beyond elaborations where clearly within band territory.

AC9TDE4K01.minimum_width: Name at least two design and technologies occupations and explain one factor — including sustainability — that has influenced a product, service or environment each occupation has produced.
AC9TDE4K01.typical_width: Examine a range of design and technologies occupations across different sectors; explain how sustainability and other factors (community need, material availability, cultural context, energy efficiency) shape what those occupations produce; describe examples of products, services and environments that reflect these factors.
wider: Examine how First Nations Australians have been and continue to be recognised for specialist design skills using local materials with sustainable practices — investigate specific historical and contemporary examples including traditional adhesives, watercraft, and built environments

Survey the design and technologies occupations in the local area (urban, suburban, regional or rural) and examine how the mix of occupations reflects local community needs — compare with an area of different geography or scale

Examine a system or service that could be improved (e.g. water-saving bathroom system, traffic management around a school, remote medical services) — analyse what design and technologies occupations would be involved and what sustainability factors would need to be considered
elaborations: exploring how many First Nations Australians were and continue to be recognised for their specialist skills in designing and producing products made from local materials and providing related services, using sustainable practices to ensure future access to meet community needs, for example traditional adhesives

exploring how design and technologies occupations in the local area (urban, suburban, regional or rural) meet community needs, for example bakers, builders, engineers, farmers, seafood industry workers, mechanics, radiographers, textile designers and others in science, technology, engineering and mathematics roles

examining the suitability of a service or system and proposing improvements, for example a water-saving system for a bathroom at home or school, traffic management systems to reduce traffic jams around the school, remote and regional services including medical services

exploring how Australian designers consider sustainability when designing products, services or environments, for example designing products from 100% recycled materials, designing services that use minimal energy, or designing landscapes that require minimal water

examining products and environments to discover the factors that may have influenced the design and, choice of technologies used, for example discussing energy-efficient cooking with a wok, or sustainable wood products for home use including furniture made from plantation timbers, bamboo toothbrushes or coconut shell bowls
conducting a survey to identify a community need that involves accessibility and social sustainability, for example design features that improve access to the school

AC9TDE4K02.minimum_width: Describe one force and one material property, and explain how they work together to affect the function of a product or system.
AC9TDE4K02.typical_width: Describe how forces (push, pull, gravity, buoyancy) and material properties (strength, flexibility, weight, hardness) affect function across different products and systems; explain how changing a force or material property would change the function.
wider: Research how First Nations Australians consider buoyant forces when selecting materials for watercraft (bark or dugout canoes) — examine how knowledge of forces and material properties is embedded in traditional design practices

Deconstruct a product or system (e.g. a Japanese bunraku puppet, a model windmill, a pop-up card) to identify all forces and material properties at work — explain how the design coordinates them to produce the intended function

Design and test a container or parachute to keep an egg intact when dropped from a height — use observations about gravity, air resistance and material properties to explain why the design works or fails; compare different design approaches
elaborations: researching how First Nations Australians consider buoyant forces as they select materials for watercraft, for example making bark or dugout canoes
looking at models to identify how materials are used and movement is created, for example in the design of a toy with wheels or moving parts

exploring through play how movement can be started by combining materials and using forces, for example releasing a wound rubber band to propel a model boat, how different materials may impact a marble roll speed, or how various surfaces from carpet to grass to concrete might affect a robot's movement
deconstructing a product or system to identify how motion and forces affect performance, for example in a puppet such as a Japanese bunraku puppet or a model windmill with moving sails

identifying engineered systems and experimenting with available local materials, tools and equipment to solve problems, for example designing a container or parachute that will keep an egg intact when dropped from a height; a pop-up card; a tower; or a vehicle

AC9TDE4K03.minimum_width: Describe one method of food production and one method of fibre production, including what tools or environments are involved in each.
AC9TDE4K03.typical_width: Describe the ways food and fibre are produced in Australia — including plant-based and animal-based food production, and animal fibres (wool, alpaca) and plant fibres (timber, cotton, bamboo); explain the tools, equipment and production environments involved in each.
wider: Research food and fibre production techniques developed by First Nations Australians — including burning, tilling, planting, transplanting, watering, weeding, thinning, cropping, storing and trading — describe how these techniques reflect sustainable production practices
Compare farming methods for food in Australia and a country in Asia — describe the different plants, animals and technologies used and explain how geography and culture shape production methods

Investigate how production of plantation timbers differs from bamboo production — compare growth rates, harvesting methods, land use and sustainability implications; discuss what makes each method suited to its context
elaborations: researching food and fibre production techniques and technologies developed by First Nations Australians, such as burning, tilling, planting, transplanting, watering, irrigating, weeding, thinning, cropping, storing and trading food

describing tools, equipment and procedures to improve plant and animal production, for example when growing vegetables in the school garden and producing environments such as a glasshouse (protected cropping) or animal housing including safe chicken shelters
comparing farming methods for food in Australia and a country in Asia, for example the use of different types of plants and animals and how diverse technologies are used to produce them

researching how animal fibres (for example wool, alpaca) and plant fibres (for example timber, cotton, bamboo) are produced in Australia, for example how production of plantation timbers may be different from bamboo production

AC9TDE4K04.minimum_width: Describe at least one way food is selected for healthy eating and one food technology (e.g. pasteurisation, freezing) that supports food safety or nutrient retention.
AC9TDE4K04.typical_width: Describe how food can be selected and prepared for healthy eating, covering nutrient content, sensory properties and seasonal availability; explain how food technologies (pasteurisation, freezing, refrigeration) support food safety and nutrient retention; compare fresh and processed foods using nutritional information.
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians consider the nutrient content of seasonal foods to maintain a balanced diet — investigate specific examples of seasonal food knowledge and discuss how this compares to contemporary nutritional guidance

Use a nutrition calculator app to compare the nutrient content of fresh ingredients against processed versions — analyse what the processing has added or removed and discuss what this means for healthy eating decisions

Explore creative food presentation — locate and discuss examples of colourful or inventive food presentation that encourages healthy eating; describe how visual appeal and sensory properties influence food selection
elaborations: exploring how First Nations Australians consider the nutrient content of seasonal foods as a means of maintaining a balanced diet

recognising the benefits food technologies provide for health and food safety and to ensure that a wide variety of food is available and can be prepared for healthy eating, for example pasteurisation of milk for food safety and freezing of vegetables to retain nutrients and reduce food waste

exploring the differences between fresh food and processed food by researching nutrient content of fresh food using a nutrition calculator app and examining nutrition information labels on processed foods for nutritional values

considering creative ways foods can be prepared for maximum taste and appeal, for example locating and discussing images online that show colourful or fun ways to present food that might encourage healthy eating
describing foods using the senses, for example describing the colour, aroma, sound, texture and taste of the ingredients in a salad or stir-fry and how our senses influence what we select to eat

AC9TDE4P01.minimum_width: Identify one design need or opportunity and test at least one material, component or process for suitability for that design purpose.
AC9TDE4P01.typical_width: Explore needs and opportunities for designing across different design contexts; test materials, components, tools, equipment and processes for suitability including sustainability considerations (compostability, durability); use test results to inform design decisions.
wider: Explore First Nations Australians' watercraft designs and their material performance — investigate how the performance of traditional designs informs new design opportunities; test equivalent materials for floating toy design

Explore materials from an Asian country context (shelters, boats, handmade tools, baskets) — test or compare materials available locally and explain how material availability and properties shape design decisions differently across cultures
Examine local products and services for design improvement opportunities — explore testing approaches for materials and processes that would be involved in an improved solution
elaborations: exploring the designs and performance of models of First Nations Australians' watercraft, and the opportunities for their designs to inform the design of a floating toy

examining the production of local products, services and environments to enhance their own design ideas, for example discussing the processes and systems that might be used to distribute hot food to a large number of people at a community event

selecting and making judgements about appropriate joining techniques for materials to produce designs, prototypes, structures or working models, for example joining fabric, paper or cardboard in various ways

exploring and testing a range of materials under different conditions for suitability including sustainability considerations, for example the compostability of paper-based materials or the strength and durability of natural materials

exploring the different uses of materials in a range of products, including those from a country in Asia, to inform design decisions, for example in shelters, boats, handmade tools, baskets, wooden items, musical instruments, clothing and fabric

AC9TDE4P02.minimum_width: Generate at least two design ideas using sketches or models and communicate one using technical terms and an annotation that explains a component's function.
AC9TDE4P02.typical_width: Generate, communicate and document design ideas using thumbnail sketches, annotated diagrams and digital tools; apply appropriate technical terms and attributions; include labels explaining materials, properties and intended function; share using digital tools with privacy considerations.
wider: Generate design ideas inspired by First Nations Australians' designs (e.g. watercraft) — acknowledge the source with attribution and describe how the traditional design informed the new idea

Generate design ideas for solutions using Safety by Design principles — produce annotated sketches showing how the design ensures accessibility for all users; explain how the safety and accessibility criteria shaped the design decisions

Communicate a design idea for a culturally specific context — research the cultural context, document the process with attributions, and reflect on how communication needed to be adapted for different audiences
elaborations: visualising innovative design ideas by producing thumbnail sketches, models and labelled drawings to explain features and modifications, for example drawing one or more designs for a machine to collect waste, and including labels and descriptions to explain materials used, their properties and the intended function of components or the whole system

planning, sharing and documenting creative designs, ideas and processes using digital tools and appropriate terms and privacy considerations, for example a class blog or collaborative document that has been selectively shared with peers

communicating design ideas using annotated diagrams, for example labelling a diagram for a pushcart with technical terms and explanations about components such as the chassis, axle, wheels and steering
generating design ideas for solutions using Safety by Design principles, for example designing communication that is accessible for all parents and carers

AC9TDE4P03.minimum_width: Select at least two materials for a design task with a stated reason for each, and demonstrate at least two safe work practices when making.
AC9TDE4P03.typical_width: Select and use materials, components, tools, equipment and techniques across different making tasks; give reasons for material and technique selections that reference properties and sustainability; apply safe, responsible and cooperative practices; use technologies terms to describe procedures.
wider: Select materials with explicit sustainability consideration — compare materials by compostability, recyclability and durability; document the reasoning and evaluate whether packaging and offcuts can be reused or recycled

Make a solution that incorporates materials from a different cultural context (e.g. bamboo, natural fibres) — describe how working with unfamiliar materials required adapting tools or techniques, and document the process using technologies terms

Explore how digital tools (virtual reality, simulations) can support safe making practice — investigate what assembly or procedure can be practised digitally before physical production and discuss the benefits and limits of this approach
elaborations: exploring ways of joining, connecting and assembling components that ensure success including the impact digital tools have on these processes, for example using virtual reality or simulations to experience assembling materials or using tools
using tools and equipment accurately when measuring, marking and cutting, for example when creating a template or pattern, measuring ingredients in a recipe or preparing a garden bed for sowing seeds
explaining the importance of safe, responsible, inclusive and cooperative work practices when designing and making, for example when handling sharp equipment such as knives and scissors

selecting and using materials, components, tools, equipment and processes with consideration of the environmental impact at each stage of the production process, for example considering how packaging and offcuts could be recycled or used for other purposes before choosing materials for a project
using appropriate technologies terms to describe and share with other students the procedures and techniques for making, for example how to safely make an engineered solution such as a robotic device

AC9TDE4P04.minimum_width: Evaluate one design idea or solution against at least two given or co-developed criteria, including one sustainability criterion, with a reason for each judgement.
AC9TDE4P04.typical_width: Use given or co-developed design criteria — including sustainability — to evaluate design ideas and solutions across different design contexts; use evaluation to revise and select between design ideas; reflect on how well the final solution meets the criteria.
wider: Co-develop design criteria that include universal design principles (flexible use, intuitive use, low physical effort) — evaluate a design against these criteria and discuss how social sustainability shapes the evaluation
Compare the waste and recyclability of different material choices using sustainability criteria — evaluate and select between design ideas based on environmental impact data
Evaluate a design solution against criteria that include competing considerations (e.g. sustainability vs durability vs cost) — reason through the trade-offs and justify the final selection
elaborations: developing design criteria with others including considering universal design principles to address social sustainability, for example a criterion that specifies flexible or intuitive use or low physical effort
using design criteria to evaluate, revise and select design ideas, for example when designing an e-textile toy for a young child to ensure it will be safe

comparing the amount of waste that would be produced from different design ideas and the potential for recycling waste, for example exploring the choice of materials to construct a toy and whether these materials are repairable or able to be recycled once the toy breaks or is no longer wanted

reflecting on how well their designed solution meets design criteria, such as ensuring safety and wellbeing of users and meeting the needs of communities or different cultures, for example reviewing and discussing the choice of fabrics used to make re-usable bags and how they could be made more appealing to all cultural groups by considering modifications to style

AC9TDE4P05.minimum_width: Record the steps for a making task in sequence using a planning tool, and contribute to a collaborative plan that allocates at least two roles with the resources each needs.
AC9TDE4P05.typical_width: Sequence steps for individual and collaborative making tasks using planning tools (timelines, lists, spreadsheets, flowcharts); manage time and resource allocation by identifying roles and their required resources; follow planned sequences to complete production.
wider: Create a flowchart for a mass production process where each student has a separate role (e.g. packing food boxes for community members) — identify decision points, parallel steps and dependencies; evaluate whether the sequence is efficient

Plan and execute a collaborative production event involving multiple roles and resources (e.g. food distribution for a community event) — reflect on where time or resource management broke down and propose improvements
Document a production sequence as a video or illustrated guide clear enough for another group to follow — evaluate the clarity and completeness of the documented steps
elaborations: determining planning processes as a class, for example recording when parts of a project need to be completed on a timeline, in a spreadsheet, calendar or list

discussing the importance of managing time and resource allocation throughout production, for example discussing the roles different people might take in a team and identifying the tasks they will complete and the resources they will each need

identifying the steps in a mass production process, for example drawing a flowchart or making a video recording of a procedure for packing identical boxes of food for community members in need, where each student in a group has a separate task as part of the production process
